entries.name: scaling hypothesis
entries.senseHere: The idea that intelligence emerges simply from making existing simple neural network designs much bigger and training them on much more data and computing power, without needing fundamentally new algorithms.

entries.name: GPT-3
entries.senseHere: The largest neural network ever trained at the time, over ten times bigger than any prior model, which unexpectedly learned to follow instructions and pick up new tasks from a few examples rather than just generating fluent text.
entries.background: Released by the AI lab OpenAI in May 2020 as the successor to GPT-2, trained on huge amounts of internet text to predict the next word in a sequence.

entries.name: meta-learning
entries.senseHere: A model's ability, once trained, to pick up and perform brand-new tasks on the fly from just a few examples in its prompt, rather than needing separate retraining for each task.

entries.name: GPT-2
entries.background: An earlier, much smaller language model from OpenAI that surprised researchers with its ability to generate coherent text and perform tasks like summarization after being trained only to predict text.

entries.name: blessings of scale
entries.senseHere: The surprising pattern where making a neural network, its training data, and its computing power larger makes training easier and more stable rather than harder, with abilities like generalization and meta-learning appearing on their own.

entries.name: Transformer
entries.background: A neural network design introduced in 2017 that processes sequences using a mechanism called self-attention, allowing it to weigh relationships between all parts of its input at once; it underlies GPT-3 and most modern large language models.

entries.name: OpenAI
entries.background: The AI research lab that built GPT-3, originally founded as a nonprofit and later restructured to include a for-profit arm so it could raise money to fund large-scale compute-intensive research.

entries.name: Hans Moravec
entries.background: A robotics researcher who in the late 20th century forecast, based on trends in computing power, that affordable hardware for human-level AI would not arrive until roughly the 2020s, a forecast that looked prescient by the time of GPT-3.

entries.name: AlphaGo Zero
entries.background: A Go-playing program from DeepMind that reached superhuman strength purely by playing against itself, without learning from any recorded human games.

entries.name: bitter lesson
entries.senseHere: The pattern that approaches relying on simply scaling up general learning methods with more computation keep beating approaches built on hand-crafted human insight into a problem.

entries.name: MuZero
entries.background: A DeepMind program that learned to plan ahead and play games like Go, chess, and Atari videogames to a superhuman level without ever being told the rules, by training a network end-to-end to predict rewards.

entries.name: OpenAI Five
entries.background: A reinforcement-learning system built by OpenAI that learned to play the video game Dota 2 competitively against professional human teams through massive-scale self-play training.

entries.name: DeepMind
entries.background: A London-based AI research lab, owned by Google, known for projects like AlphaGo and for favoring piece-by-piece, neuroscience-inspired approaches to building intelligent systems.

entries.name: pretraining thesis
entries.senseHere: The argument that if a model is trained hard enough to predict text as accurately as a human would, it must eventually acquire real understanding of logic, causality, and the world, because nothing less would let it match human-level prediction on the hardest, rarest cases.

entries.name: hardware overhang
entries.senseHere: A situation where computing hardware powerful enough to train a major new capability already exists and is affordable, but no one has yet applied it, meaning a big capability jump can happen suddenly once someone does.

entries.name: Ilya Sutskever
entries.background: A deep learning researcher and OpenAI's chief scientist, known for early contributions to neural network training and for strongly backing the idea that scaling up existing methods would unlock new capabilities.

entries.name: intentional stance
entries.senseHere: Treating a system as if it has goals and beliefs because doing so predicts its behavior more easily than tracing every underlying physical step, which the piece argues a large enough model may adopt internally even for 'non-agentic' systems.
entries.background: A term coined by the philosopher Daniel Dennett for the strategy of explaining or predicting a system's behavior by attributing to it beliefs, desires, and rationality, rather than describing its internal mechanics.

entries.name: Daniel Dennett
entries.background: A philosopher known for his work on mind and cognition, including proposing that treating complex systems as goal-pursuing agents can be a useful predictive shortcut even when those systems have no literal intentions.

entries.name: Conway's Game of Life
entries.background: A simple cellular automaton where cells on a grid turn on or off each step following a few fixed rules, yet it generates complex recurring patterns like 'gliders' that drift across the grid as if they were objects.

entries.name: Turing machine
entries.background: A simple mathematical model of computation consisting of rules for reading, writing, and moving along an infinite tape, used as the theoretical basis for what counts as 'computable.'
